claim: Under eubiotic conditions commensal microbes provide a competitive barrier against invading bacterial pathogens in the intestinal tract, on the skin or on the vaginal mucosa.
source: Under eubiotic conditions commensal microbes are known to provide a competitive barrier against invading bacterial pathogens in the intestinal tract, on the skin or on the vaginal mucosa.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge in the abstract without specific citations in this sentence.

claim: In eubiosis, the lungs of mice were dominantly colonized by Lactobacillus murinus.
source: In eubiosis, the lungs of mice were dominantly colonized by Lactobacillus murinus.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Differential analysis of 16S rRNA gene sequencing or L. murinus-specific qPCR of DNA from total organ homogenates vs. broncho alveolar lavages implicated tight association of these bacteria with the host tissue.
source: Differential analysis of 16S rRNA gene sequencing or L. murinus-specific qPCR of DNA from total organ homogenates vs.broncho alveolar lavages implicated tight association of these bacteria with the host tissue.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data comparing different sampling methods.

claim: Pure L. murinus conditioned culture medium inhibited growth of S. pneumoniae.
source: Pure L. murinus conditioned culture medium inhibited growth and reduced the extension of pneumococcal chains.
evidence: This is a primary experimental finding stated in the abstract and supported by in vitro data.

claim: Pure L. murinus conditioned culture medium reduced the extension of pneumococcal chains.
source: Pure L. murinus conditioned culture medium inhibited growth and reduced the extension of pneumococcal chains.
evidence: This is a primary experimental finding stated in the abstract and supported by in vitro data.

claim: Growth inhibition in vitro was likely dependent on L. murinus-produced lactic acid.
source: Growth inhibition in vitro was likely dependent on L. murinus-produced lactic acid, since pH neutralization of the conditioned medium aborted the antibacterial effect.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data showing pH neutralization effects.

claim: pH neutralization of the conditioned medium aborted the antibacterial effect.
source: Growth inhibition in vitro was likely dependent on L. murinus-produced lactic acid, since pH neutralization of the conditioned medium aborted the antibacterial effect.
evidence: This is experimental data supporting the lactic acid mechanism.

claim: L. murinus provides a barrier against pneumococcal colonization in a respiratory dysbiosis model after an influenza A virus infection, when added therapeutically.
source: Finally, we demonstrate that L. murinus provides a barrier against pneumococcal colonization in a respiratory dysbiosis model after an influenza A virus infection, when added therapeutically.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by in vivo experimental data.

claim: In the densely colonized gut, commensal bacteria confer a prominent protective role against invading bacterial pathogens, in part by posing a competitive threshold within this ecological niche.
source: In the densely colonized gut, commensal bacteria confer a prominent protective role against invading bacterial pathogens, in part by posing a competitive threshold within this ecological niche (Barthel et al., 2003).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Barthel et al., 2003.

claim: The biological barrier provided by commensal bacteria is absent in axenic mice.
source: This biological barrier is absent in axenic mice and reduced in mice harboring a low-complexity microbiota colonized mice.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge based on the context of the introduction.

claim: The biological barrier provided by commensal bacteria is reduced in mice harboring a low-complexity microbiota.
source: This biological barrier is absent in axenic mice and reduced in mice harboring a low-complexity microbiota colonized mice.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge based on the context of the introduction.

claim: Barrier function of the microbiota is sensitive to antibiotics treatment in colonized conventionally housed mice.
source: Barrier function of the microbiota is consequently sensitive to antibiotics treatment in colonized conventionally housed mice (Barthel et al., 2003; Brugiroux et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Barthel et al., 2003 and Brugiroux et al., 2017.

claim: Skin microbiota poses a barrier against colonization by bacterial skin pathogens.
source: Skin microbiota poses a similar barrier against colonization by bacterial skin pathogens (reviewed in Parlet et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a review by Parlet et al., 2019.

claim: The lower respiratory tract was previously considered quasi-sterile.
source: In recent years, it became evident that the lower respiratory tract (LRT), previously considered quasi-sterile, also hosts a bacterial microbiota under healthy conditions (Dickson et al., 2015).
evidence: This is stated as historical context in the introduction.

claim: The lower respiratory tract hosts a bacterial microbiota under healthy conditions.
source: In recent years, it became evident that the lower respiratory tract (LRT), previously considered quasi-sterile, also hosts a bacterial microbiota under healthy conditions (Dickson et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Dickson et al., 2015.

claim: Compositional changes occur in the intestinal microbiota over the course of an IAV infection in C57BL/6J mice housed under SPF conditions.
source: Recently, a number of groups, including ours, reported compositional changes in the intestinal and lower respiratory tract microbiota over the course of an IAV infection using a C57BL/6J mouse model housed under specific pathogen-free (SPF) conditions (Deriu et al., 2016; Groves et al., 2018; Planet et al., 2016; Yildiz et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations including the authors' own work.

claim: Compositional changes occur in the lower respiratory tract microbiota over the course of an IAV infection in C57BL/6J mice housed under SPF conditions.
source: Recently, a number of groups, including ours, reported compositional changes in the intestinal and lower respiratory tract microbiota over the course of an IAV infection using a C57BL/6J mouse model housed under specific pathogen-free (SPF) conditions (Deriu et al., 2016; Groves et al., 2018; Planet et al., 2016; Yildiz et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations including the authors' own work.

claim: IAV infection opens a temporarily limited window for Salmonella enterica serovar Typhimurium infection in the intestine.
source: This opened a temporarily limited window for Salmonella enterica serovar Typhimurium infection in the intestine, similarly as in mice orally treated with antibiotics (Deriu et al., 2016; Yildiz et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Deriu et al., 2016 and Yildiz et al., 2018.

claim: Little qualitative or quantitative differences were found in respiratory microbiota of IAV infected mice by 16S rRNA gene-specific next generation sequencing and qPCR.
source: We found only little qualitative or quantitative differences in respiratory microbiota of IAV infected mice by 16S rRNA gene-specific next generation sequencing and qPCR.
evidence: This is a finding from the authors' previous work.

claim: Enhanced secondary colonization with Streptococcus pneumoniae occurs following IAV infections.
source: Nevertheless, we observed enhanced secondary colonization with Streptococcus pneumoniae following IAV infections, as described previously (McCullers and Rehg, 2002).
evidence: This claim is supported by the authors' data and a citation to McCullers and Rehg, 2002.

claim: The outcome of IAV-bacterial super-infections is determined by host factors, viral factors and factors of the bacterial pathogen.
source: The outcome of these super-infections is determined by host factors, viral factors and factors of the bacterial pathogen (reviewed in McCullers, 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a review by McCullers, 2014.

claim: Bacterial colonization of the lung is important to prime alveolar macrophages.
source: IAV infections take place in the poly-microbial environment of the respiratory tract and bacterial colonization of the lung is important to prime alveolar macrophages (Abt et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Abt et al., 2012.

claim: A high content of Lactobacillaceae was discovered in the lung microbiota of healthy SPF housed mice.
source: We recently discovered a high content of Lactobacillaceae in the lung microbiota of healthy SPF housed mice, which was not reported before (Yildiz et al., 2018).
evidence: This is a finding from the authors' previous work cited as Yildiz et al., 2018.

claim: The lung-isolated bacterial strains clustered with L. murinus based on 16S rRNA gene phylogeny.
source: The lung-isolated strains clustered with L. murinus and were clearly separated from L. animalis and L. apodemi isolates.
evidence: This claim is supported by phylogenetic analysis data shown in Figure 1A.

claim: The lung-isolated bacterial strains were clearly separated from L. animalis and L. apodemi isolates based on 16S rRNA gene phylogeny.
source: The lung-isolated strains clustered with L. murinus and were clearly separated from L. animalis and L. apodemi isolates.
evidence: This claim is supported by phylogenetic analysis data shown in Figure 1A.

claim: L. murinus ASF361 was the best match to the lung isolate based on genome alignment.
source: Blasting of the de novo assembled genome against available genomes revealed that indeed L. murinus ASF361 was the best match to our L. murinus strain isolate (Figure 1B, z-score = 1, PRJNA591640 and Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by genome alignment data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Alignment of the whole genome of the Lactobacillus isolate to the reference genome of L. murinus ASF361 resulted in >99.5% sequence identity.
source: Alignment of the whole genome of our Lactobacillus isolate to the recently published reference genome of L. murinus ASF361 (Wannemuehler et al., 2014) resulted in >99. 5% sequence identity (Figure 1C).
evidence: This claim is supported by genome alignment data shown in Figure 1C and cites Wannemuehler et al., 2014.

claim: Previous analyses of murine LRT microbiota by 16S rRNA gene NGS revealed a higher diversity with a balanced distribution of Actinobacteria, Bacteroidetes, Firmicutes and Proteobacteria.
source: Previous analyses of murine LRT microbiota by 16S rRNA gene NGS revealed a higher diversity with a balanced distribution of Actinobacteria, Bacteroidetes, Firmicutes and Proteobacteria (Barfod et al., 2013; Poroyko et al., 2015; Singh et al., 2017; Yadava et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to previous studies.

claim: Differences in sampling techniques might introduce a potential sampling bias by avoiding or limiting tissue-associated bacteria.
source: We speculated that differences in sampling techniques (bronchoalveolar lavage fluid (BALF) vs. partial organs vs. total organs) might introduce a potential sampling bias by avoiding or limiting tissue-associated bacteria.
evidence: This is a speculation by the authors to explain discrepancies in the literature.

claim: Lactobacillaceae were predominantly found in total organ samples.
source: As demonstrated before (Yildiz et al., 2018), we found predominantly Lactobacillaceae in total organ samples (Figure 2A/B).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 2A/B and cites the authors' previous work.

claim: Lactobacillaceae were poorly represented in BALF samples, indicating a tight association with lung tissue.
source: However, this family was poorly represented in BALF samples, indicating a tight association with lung tissue.
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 2 and represents an inference from the sampling comparison.

claim: Alpha diversity was higher in BALF samples compared to tissue samples.
source: Accordingly, alpha diversity was higher in BALF samples (Figure 2C) and the overall homogeneous composition of BALF microbiota confirmed previous analysis by other groups.
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: Total 16S copy numbers by qPCR were substantially higher in tissue-derived samples than in BALF samples.
source: Of note, total 16S copy numbers by qPCR on the same amount of input DNA were substantially higher in tissue-derived samples (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A) than in BALF samples.
evidence: This claim is supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1A.

claim: BALF samples were indistinguishable from blanks and background by 16S rRNA-specific qPCR.
source: Effectively, BALF samples were indistinguishable from blanks and background by 16S rRNA-specific qPCR.
evidence: This is an observation from the qPCR data analysis.

claim: BALF samples were distinct in bacterial composition and abundance from tissue homogenates based on beta-diversity analysis.
source: Beta-diversity (Weighted UniFrac) analysis revealed that BALF samples were found to be distinct in bacterial composition and abundance from tissue homogenates, resembling largely blank samples in SPF housed and separately positioned in CONV housed mice (Figure 2D).
evidence: This claim is supported by beta-diversity analysis shown in Figure 2D.

claim: Four out of five SPF mice displayed DNA equivalent to >10e7 cfu/lung of L. murinus.
source: Four out of five SPF mice displayed DNA equivalent to >10e7 cfu/lung (Figure 3A and Figure 3—figure supplement 1B), which was about 100–1000 fold higher than the titers of life L. murinus determined by plating of lung homogenates (Yildiz et al., 2018) and potentially a result of dead L. murinus.
evidence: This claim is supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 3A and Figure 3—figure supplement 1B.

claim: L. murinus DNA levels detected by qPCR were about 100-1000 fold higher than the titers of live L. murinus determined by plating of lung homogenates.
source: Four out of five SPF mice displayed DNA equivalent to >10e7 cfu/lung (Figure 3A and Figure 3—figure supplement 1B), which was about 100–1000 fold higher than the titers of life L. murinus determined by plating of lung homogenates (Yildiz et al., 2018) and potentially a result of dead L. murinus.
evidence: This claim compares qPCR data to previous plating data and cites Yildiz et al., 2018.

claim: The discrepancy between DNA levels and viable counts is potentially a result of dead L. murinus.
source: Four out of five SPF mice displayed DNA equivalent to >10e7 cfu/lung (Figure 3A and Figure 3—figure supplement 1B), which was about 100–1000 fold higher than the titers of life L. murinus determined by plating of lung homogenates (Yildiz et al., 2018) and potentially a result of dead L. murinus.
evidence: This is a speculation by the authors to explain the discrepancy between DNA and viable counts.

claim: L. murinus was not detected in DNA of BALF samples by L. murinus-specific qPCR.
source: In line with the 16S rRNA NGS date (Figure 2A) we did not detect L. murinus in DNA of BALF samples by L. murinus-specific qPCR, but in the majority of total lung DNA and DNA from lungs after BAL (Figure 3B).
evidence: This claim is supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: L. murinus was detected in the majority of total lung DNA and DNA from lungs after BAL by L. murinus-specific qPCR.
source: In line with the 16S rRNA NGS date (Figure 2A) we did not detect L. murinus in DNA of BALF samples by L. murinus-specific qPCR, but in the majority of total lung DNA and DNA from lungs after BAL (Figure 3B).
evidence: This claim is supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: L. murinus was exclusively visible in the airway space of SPF mouse lungs by RNAScope ISH.
source: Bright red staining for L. murinus was exclusively visible in the airway space of SPF mouse lungs, but not in the germfree control specimen (Figure 3C).
evidence: This claim is supported by ISH data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: L. murinus was not visible in germfree control specimens by RNAScope ISH.
source: Bright red staining for L. murinus was exclusively visible in the airway space of SPF mouse lungs, but not in the germfree control specimen (Figure 3C).
evidence: This claim is supported by ISH data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: L. murinus was predominantly found in large airways of the bronchi, but not in the trachea or the alveolar space.
source: L. murinus was predominantely found in large airways of the bronchi, but not in the trachea or the alveolar space (upper panels).
evidence: This claim is supported by ISH data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: L. murinus-specific staining showed overall good correlation with total eubacterial staining.
source: Staining of adjacent slides for eubacteria (lower panels), revealed overall good correlation of L. murinus-specific staining with total eubacterial staining.
evidence: This claim is supported by comparison of ISH staining patterns shown in Figure 3C.

claim: The RNAScope data support that L. murinus is viable in the lung.
source: The RNAScope data further support that L. murinus is viable in the lung, since we detected short lived bacterial RNA.
evidence: This is an inference based on the detection of RNA by RNAScope.

claim: Members of the family Lactobacillaceae were previously shown to inhibit growth of Gram-positive or Gram-negative bacteria in co-culture or by exposure to Lactobacillus conditioned medium.
source: Members of the family Lactobacillaceae were previously shown to inhibit growth of Gram-positive or Gram-negative bacteria in co-culture or by exposure to Lactobacillus conditioned medium (De Keersmaecker et al., 2006; Lu et al., 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to De Keersmaecker et al., 2006 and Lu et al., 2009.

claim: L. murinus conditioned MRS medium (LmCM) inhibited growth of S. pneumoniae cultures.
source: Only LmCM inhibited growth of S. pneumoniae cultures that prevented reaching the same optical density, even after prolonged incubation, compared S. pneumoniae grown in FM or EcCM supplemented TSB (Figure 4A).
evidence: This claim is supported by growth curve data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: E. coli conditioned medium (EcCM) did not inhibit growth of S. pneumoniae cultures.
source: Only LmCM inhibited growth of S. pneumoniae cultures that prevented reaching the same optical density, even after prolonged incubation, compared S. pneumoniae grown in FM or EcCM supplemented TSB (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is inferred from the comparison showing only LmCM had an effect, implying EcCM did not.

claim: LmCM caused a one log magnitude reduction of S. pneumoniae viability compared to FM or EcCM.
source: To decipher between the two possibilities, we conducted efficiency of plating assays of serially diluted S. pneumoniae cultures grown for 6 hr in FM, LmCM, or EcCM and found a one log in magnitude reduction of viability with LmCM compared to the other conditions, confirming the reduction in bacterial growth (Figure 4B,C).
evidence: This claim is supported by plating assay data shown in Figure 4B,C.

claim: L. murinus produces a soluble killing activity that acts on S. pneumoniae.
source: This result suggests a soluble killing activity produced by L. murinus that acts on S. pneumoniae.
evidence: This is an inference based on the conditioned medium experiments.

claim: Inhibition of S. pneumoniae by LmCM is strain independent.
source: Our results indicate that inhibition of S. pneumoniae by LmCM is strain independent and is not affected by capsule formation since both strains displayed similar sensitivity to LmCM as the virulent encapsulated strain (ATCC6303) (Figure 4B–D).
evidence: This claim is supported by data testing multiple S. pneumoniae strains shown in Figure 4D.

claim: Inhibition of S. pneumoniae by LmCM is not affected by capsule formation.
source: Our results indicate that inhibition of S. pneumoniae by LmCM is strain independent and is not affected by capsule formation since both strains displayed similar sensitivity to LmCM as the virulent encapsulated strain (ATCC6303) (Figure 4B–D).
evidence: This claim is supported by data comparing encapsulated and non-encapsulated strains shown in Figure 4D.

claim: LmCM reduced optical density of S. aureus cultures.
source: Despite the much faster in vitro growth rate, LmCM reduced optical density of S. aureus cultures (Figure 4E), implicating a broader acting mechanism against at least two distinct pathogenic bacteria.
evidence: This claim is supported by growth data shown in Figure 4E.

claim: LmCM has a broader acting mechanism against at least two distinct pathogenic bacteria.
source: Despite the much faster in vitro growth rate, LmCM reduced optical density of S. aureus cultures (Figure 4E), implicating a broader acting mechanism against at least two distinct pathogenic bacteria.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that LmCM affects both S. pneumoniae and S. aureus.

claim: Encapsulated S. pneumoniae forms linear chains in vitro and in vivo.
source: Encapsulated S. pneumonia forms linear chains in vitro and in vivo.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about S. pneumoniae.

claim: Formation of chains was previously associated with tissue adhesion and pathogenicity in vivo.
source: Formation of chains was previously associated with tissue adhesion and pathogenicity in vivo (Rodriguez et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Rodriguez et al., 2012.

claim: A significant decrease in median chain length of S. pneumoniae was observed when grown in the presence of LmCM.
source: We observed a significant decrease in median chain length of S. pneumonia when grown in the presence of LmCM (Figure 5A/B).
evidence: This claim is supported by microscopy data shown in Figure 5A/B.

claim: EcCM did not affect S. pneumoniae growth or chain length.
source: EcCM, however, did not affect S. pneumoniae growth and/or chain length.
evidence: This is stated based on the experimental results shown in Figure 5.

claim: Proteinase K treatment had no effect on LmCM's S. pneumoniae growth inhibition.
source: In order to narrow down the nature of the soluble inhibitor of S. pneumoniae growth, we first treated the LmCM with Proteinase K. This treatment had no effect on its S. pneumoniae growth inhibition (Figure 5—figure supplement 1), excluding e.g. the action of bacteriocins.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: The action of bacteriocins is excluded as the mechanism of growth inhibition.
source: In order to narrow down the nature of the soluble inhibitor of S. pneumoniae growth, we first treated the LmCM with Proteinase K. This treatment had no effect on its S. pneumoniae growth inhibition (Figure 5—figure supplement 1), excluding e.g. the action of bacteriocins.
evidence: This is an inference based on the proteinase K treatment results.

claim: The active compound affecting S. pneumoniae growth in vitro could be a small bacterial metabolite.
source: Our results suggested the active compound affecting S. pneumoniae growth in vitro could be a small bacterial metabolite.
evidence: This is a speculation based on the proteinase K results.

claim: 174 metabolite features were at least 10-fold enriched in LmCM over FM and not upregulated in EcCM.
source: 174 metabolite features that are at least 10-fold enriched in LmCM over in FM and not upregulated in EcCM (Figure 5—figure supplement 1) were detected.
evidence: This claim is supported by metabolomics data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: D-Glucosamine-6-phosphate and uridine-diphosphate-glucose were unambiguously identified in LmCM by comparison to reference chemical standards.
source: Two of these peaks were unambiguously identified by comparison to reference chemical standards: D-Glucosamine-6-phosphate and uridine-diphosphate-glucose.
evidence: This claim is supported by metabolomics analysis using chemical standards.

claim: Exposure of S. pneumoniae to D-Glucosamine-6-phosphate or uridine-diphosphate-glucose in concentrations up to 10 mM did not affect bacterial growth.
source: However, exposure of S. pneumoniae to these metabolites in concentrations up to 10 mM did not affect bacterial growth (Figure 5—figure supplement 2), making it unlikely that any of these putative L. murinus metabolites are responsible for the observed inhibition of S. pneumoniae growth.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2.

claim: Some Lactobacillus species produce high levels of H2O2 when grown in presence of oxygen.
source: Some Lactobacillus species were previously reported to produce high levels of H2O2 when grown in presence of oxygen (Hertzberger et al., 2014; Kang et al., 2013; Marty-Teysset et al., 2000).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Supernatants of L. murinus grown in hypoxia showed similar levels of growth inhibition as those grown in normoxia.
source: However, supernatants of L. murinus grown in hypoxia showed similar levels of growth inhibition (Figure 5—figure supplement 3A).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 3A.

claim: Catalase treatment did not affect the growth arrest on S. pneumoniae seen with LmCM.
source: Moreover, catalase treatment did not affect the growth arrest on S. pneumoniae seen with LmCM, while it completely abolished the effect of H2O2 (Figure 5—figure supplement 3B).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 3B.

claim: Catalase treatment completely abolished the effect of H2O2 on S. pneumoniae growth.
source: Moreover, catalase treatment did not affect the growth arrest on S. pneumoniae seen with LmCM, while it completely abolished the effect of H2O2 (Figure 5—figure supplement 3B).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 3B.

claim: Reactive oxygen species are excluded from the candidate list of active metabolites in LmCM.
source: These results excluded reactive oxygen species from the candidate list of active metabolites in LmCM.
evidence: This is an inference based on the hypoxia and catalase treatment results.

claim: LmCM had a pH of 4.5.
source: Of note, LmCM had a pH of 4.5 (Figure 6A).
evidence: This claim is supported by pH measurement data shown in Figure 6A.

claim: A full recovery of S. pneumoniae growth was observed when the LmCM was pH neutralized with NaOH.
source: We observed a full recovery of S. pneumoniae growth, when the LCM was pH neutralized with NaOH (Figure 6B).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6B.

claim: Lactic acid might be the compound responsible for the antimicrobial action of LmCM.
source: We thus speculated that indeed lactic acid might be the compound responsible for the antimicrobial action of LmCM.
evidence: This is a speculation based on the pH neutralization results.

claim: Quantification of lactic acid in LmCM by GC/MS revealed concentrations of approximately 100 µM.
source: Indeed, quantification of lactic acid in LmCM by GC/MS revealed concentrations of approximately 100 µM (Figure 6C).
evidence: This claim is supported by GC/MS data shown in Figure 6C.

claim: 100 µM DL-lactic acid inhibited S. pneumoniae growth at comparable levels to LmCM.
source: In order to test if these concentrations are sufficient to explain the antibacterial effect of LmCM, we grew S. pneumoniae for 6 hr in TSB complemented with 100 µM DL-lactic acid. Indeed, we observed inhibition of S. pneumoniae growth at comparable levels to LmCM (Figure 6D), sustained over 24 hr (data not shown).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6D.

claim: Lactic acid is the primary metabolite in LmCM causing growth arrest on S. pneumoniae.
source: These results suggest that lactic acid is the primary metabolite in LmCM causing growth arrest on S. pneumoniae.
evidence: This is an inference based on the lactic acid supplementation experiments.

claim: The reduction of median chain length of S. pneumoniae cultures by LmCM was not affected by presence of lactic acid.
source: The second phenotype induced by LmCM, the reduction of median chain length of S. pneumoniae cultures (see Figure 4a), was not affected by presence of lactic acid (Figure 7A).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7A.

claim: pH neutralization did not restore S. pneumoniae chain length.
source: Accordingly, pH neutralization did not restore chain length (Figure 7B).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7B.

claim: The effect of lactic acid on S. pneumoniae growth in vitro is independent of the inhibition of chain length.
source: This implies that the effect of lactic acid on S. pneumoniae growth in vitro is independent of the previously observed inhibition of chain length.
evidence: This is an inference based on the lactic acid and pH neutralization experiments.

claim: Proteinase K completely abolished the reduced chain extension caused by LmCM.
source: In order to characterize the nature of the compound responsible for inhibition of chain extension we repeated the treatment of LmCM with protease K. Proteinase K completely abolished the reduced chain extension (Figure 7C), suggesting a secreted protein or peptide could be responsible for disrupting or preventing chain formation.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7C.

claim: A secreted protein or peptide could be responsible for disrupting or preventing S. pneumoniae chain formation.
source: In order to characterize the nature of the compound responsible for inhibition of chain extension we repeated the treatment of LmCM with protease K. Proteinase K completely abolished the reduced chain extension (Figure 7C), suggesting a secreted protein or peptide could be responsible for disrupting or preventing chain formation.
evidence: This is a speculation based on the proteinase K treatment results.

claim: Germ-free mice were not more susceptible to S. pneumoniae colonization than colonized SPF mice.
source: To our great surprise we did not find increased susceptibility of GF mice to S. pneumoniae infection over colonized SPF mice (Figure 8A).
evidence: This claim is supported by in vivo infection data shown in Figure 8A.

claim: Germ-free mice were resistant to S. pneumoniae colonization, largely independent of L. murinus pretreatment.
source: In fact, GF mice were resistant to colonization, largely independent of L. murinus pretreatment.
evidence: This claim is supported by in vivo infection data shown in Figure 8A.

claim: Resistance of germ-free mice to S. pneumoniae colonization did not correlate with significantly lowered lung pH.
source: Resistance did not correlate with significantly lowered lung pH (Figure 8B).
evidence: This claim is supported by pH measurement data shown in Figure 8B.

claim: In colonized SPF mice, pretreatment with L. murinus had a small but statistically non-significant effect on S. pneumoniae colonization.
source: In colonized SPF mice, the pretreatment with L. murinus had a small but statistically non-significant effect on S. pneumoniae colonization (Figure 8A), which is likely due to the already present population of respiratory commensal L. murinus.
evidence: This claim is supported by in vivo infection data shown in Figure 8A.

claim: The small effect of L. murinus pretreatment in SPF mice is likely due to the already present population of respiratory commensal L. murinus.
source: In colonized SPF mice, the pretreatment with L. murinus had a small but statistically non-significant effect on S. pneumoniae colonization (Figure 8A), which is likely due to the already present population of respiratory commensal L. murinus.
evidence: This is a speculation to explain the lack of effect in SPF mice.

claim: L. murinus instillation did not alter body weight of the mice.
source: Of note, L. murinus instillation did not alter body weight of the mice, which indicates no adverse effects by this probiotic treatment.
evidence: This is an observation from the in vivo experiments.

claim: IAV infection lowers the natural colonization threshold to S. pneumoniae in SPF mice.
source: Even in SPF mice, the colonization of the respiratory tract with low doses of S. pneumoniae is quite inefficient. This natural colonization threshold can be lowered by previous, sub-lethal IAV infection (Figure 8B), modeling the frequently observed secondary bacterial pneumonia in human IAV patients (Morris et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by in vivo infection data shown in Figure 8B and cites Morris et al., 2017.

claim: Inoculating IAV infected mice on day 7 post-infection with L. murinus via the intranasal route resulted in a significant reduction in BALF pH.
source: When inoculating IAV infected mice on day 7-post infection (after onset of clinical signs of IAV infection) with L. murinus via the intranasal route, we observed a significant reduction BALF pH and diminished pneumococcal colonization on day 11-post IAV infection (24 hr post secondary S. pneumoniae challenge) (Figure 8C/D).
evidence: This claim is supported by in vivo data shown in Figure 8C/D.

claim: Inoculating IAV infected mice on day 7 post-infection with L. murinus via the intranasal route resulted in diminished pneumococcal colonization on day 11 post-IAV infection.
source: When inoculating IAV infected mice on day 7-post infection (after onset of clinical signs of IAV infection) with L. murinus via the intranasal route, we observed a significant reduction BALF pH and diminished pneumococcal colonization on day 11-post IAV infection (24 hr post secondary S. pneumoniae challenge) (Figure 8C/D).
evidence: This claim is supported by in vivo data shown in Figure 8C/D.

claim: Lactic acid levels in BALF were not changed after L. murinus colonization compared to IAV infected and mock colonized controls.
source: Lactic acid levels in BALF of these mice were not changed compared to IAV infected and mock colonized controls (Figure 8—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This claim is supported by lactic acid measurement data shown in Figure 8—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Treatment with L. murinus did not influence the overall pathology of IAV infection as indicated by similar weight loss in both experimental groups.
source: Importantly, treatment with L. murinus did not influence the overall pathology of IAV infection as indicated by similar weight loss in both experimental groups (Figure 8—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This claim is supported by body weight data shown in Figure 8—figure supplement 1C.

claim: Lactobacilli were previously shown to modulate inflammatory signaling.
source: Lactobacilli were previously shown to modulate inflammatory signaling.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge without a specific citation in this sentence.

claim: An involvement of the innate host protein response was ruled out by specific qPCR for key cytokines involved in antibacterial signaling.
source: An involvement of the innate host protein response was ruled out by specific qPCR for key cytokines involved in antibacterial signaling (Figure 8—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This claim is supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 8—figure supplement 1B.

claim: IAV infected mice showed a robust inflammatory response in their lungs on D10 post infection.
source: IAV infected mice showed a robust inflammatory response in their lungs on D10 post infection, which was non-significantly impacted by administration of L. murinus.
evidence: This is an observation from the cytokine qPCR data.

claim: The inflammatory response in IAV infected mice was non-significantly impacted by administration of L. murinus.
source: IAV infected mice showed a robust inflammatory response in their lungs on D10 post infection, which was non-significantly impacted by administration of L. murinus.
evidence: This is an observation from the cytokine qPCR data.

claim: A mild increase in Bacilli was found in SPF mice colonized with L. murinus.
source: Indeed, we found a mild increase in Bacilli in SPF mice colonized with L. murinus and a homogenous reduction of the remaining bacterial classes (Figure 8—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This claim is supported by 16S rRNA gene sequencing data shown in Figure 8—figure supplement 1C.

claim: A homogenous reduction of the remaining bacterial classes was found in SPF mice colonized with L. murinus.
source: Indeed, we found a mild increase in Bacilli in SPF mice colonized with L. murinus and a homogenous reduction of the remaining bacterial classes (Figure 8—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This claim is supported by 16S rRNA gene sequencing data shown in Figure 8—figure supplement 1C.

claim: The overall composition of lung microbiota was indistinguishable between mock and L. murinus colonized mice as indicated by largely overlapping clouds in the PCoA.
source: The overall composition of lung microbiota was however indistinguishable as indicated by largely overlapping clouds in the PCoA (Figure 8—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This claim is supported by beta-diversity analysis shown in Figure 8—figure supplement 1D.

claim: L. murinus could be a safe and directly acting antibacterial probiotic candidate for the respiratory tract.
source: These data indicate that L. murinus could be a safe and directly acting antibacterial probiotic candidate for the respiratory tract.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the in vivo safety and efficacy data.

claim: L. murinus was reported to colonize the intestine in laboratory mice.
source: In laboratory mice, L. murinus, as part of the ASF, was reported to colonize the intestine (Almirón et al., 2013; Hemme et al., 1980), the oral cavity (Blais and Lavoie, 1990; Rodrigue et al., 1993) and the vaginal tract (Jerse et al., 2002).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to previous studies.

claim: L. murinus was reported to colonize the oral cavity in laboratory mice.
source: In laboratory mice, L. murinus, as part of the ASF, was reported to colonize the intestine (Almirón et al., 2013; Hemme et al., 1980), the oral cavity (Blais and Lavoie, 1990; Rodrigue et al., 1993) and the vaginal tract (Jerse et al., 2002).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Blais and Lavoie, 1990 and Rodrigue et al., 1993.

claim: L. murinus was reported to colonize the vaginal tract in laboratory mice.
source: In laboratory mice, L. murinus, as part of the ASF, was reported to colonize the intestine (Almirón et al., 2013; Hemme et al., 1980), the oral cavity (Blais and Lavoie, 1990; Rodrigue et al., 1993) and the vaginal tract (Jerse et al., 2002).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Jerse et al., 2002.

claim: L. murinus was not reported as a dominant species in the lower respiratory tract prior to this study.
source: In the lower respiratory tract L. murinus was to our best knowledge not reported as a dominant species, however Lactobacilli were previously found in high number in lung tissue microbiome (Singh et al., 2017; Zhang et al., 2018).
evidence: This is stated by the authors based on their literature review.

claim: Lactobacilli were previously found in high number in lung tissue microbiome.
source: In the lower respiratory tract L. murinus was to our best knowledge not reported as a dominant species, however Lactobacilli were previously found in high number in lung tissue microbiome (Singh et al., 2017; Zhang et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Singh et al., 2017 and Zhang et al., 2018.

claim: The sampling technique is critical for the adequate quantification of L. murinus in the lung, since they might have a tight association with the host tissue.
source: Our data implicate that the sampling technique is critical for the adequate quantification of this species in the lung, since they might have a tight association with the host tissue.
evidence: This is an inference based on the comparison of sampling methods.

claim: A previous comparison of BALF with lung tissue revealed enrichment of Firmicutes in tissue.
source: A previous comparison of BALF (+ or - cells) with lung tissue (from the distal tips of the lung) revealed enrichment of Firmicutes in tissue (Barfod et al., 2013), independently confirming our observation.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Barfod et al., 2013.

claim: A substantial proportion of commensal bacteria in BAL samples of human patients is tightly associated with cells and thus easily lost during removal of these cells.
source: Even within BAL samples of human patients, it was previously reported that a substantial proportion of commensal bacteria is tightly associated with cells and thus easily lost during removal of these cells (Dickson et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Dickson et al., 2014.

claim: Lactobacilli are still overall dominant in the lung tissue microbiome of conventionally housed mice after two weeks of open cage housing.
source: From conventionally housed mice in our own facility, we know that Lactobacilli are still overall dominant in the lung tissue microbiome after two weeks of open cage housing.
evidence: This is an observation from the authors' own experiments.

claim: Colonization of GF mice with Lactobacillus spp. was proposed to increase alveoli numbers per µm2.
source: Colonization of GF mice with Lactobacillus spp. was proposed to increased alveoli numbers per µm2 and to enhanced mucus production after 16 weeks (Yun et al., 2014), comparable to non-SPF mice, albeit this was not independently confirmed by others.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Yun et al., 2014, but noted as not independently confirmed.

claim: Colonization of GF mice with Lactobacillus spp. was proposed to enhance mucus production after 16 weeks.
source: Colonization of GF mice with Lactobacillus spp. was proposed to increased alveoli numbers per µm2 and to enhanced mucus production after 16 weeks (Yun et al., 2014), comparable to non-SPF mice, albeit this was not independently confirmed by others.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Yun et al., 2014, but noted as not independently confirmed.

claim: Intranasal application of L. rhamnosus GG or L. paracasei reduces IL-5 and eotaxin production in the lung.
source: Intranasal application of L. rhamnosus GG or L. paracasei one reduces IL-5 and eotaxin production in the lung (Pellaton et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Pellaton et al., 2012.

claim: Intranasal application of L. rhamnosus GG was shown to suppress allergic responses in mouse models.
source: Intranasal application of L. rhamnosus GG was recently shown to suppress allergic responses in mouse models (Spacova et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Spacova et al., 2019.

claim: Colonization with L. murinus H12 was described to protect neonatal rats from necrotizing enterocolitis.
source: Colonization with L. murinus H12 was recently described to protect neonatal rats from necrotizing enterocolitis (Isani et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Isani et al., 2018.

claim: Lactobacilli produce antimicrobial peptides such as bacteriocins.
source: Lactobacilli produce antimicrobial peptides such as bacteriocins (Elayaraja et al., 2014) and metabolites that are antibacterial in nature such as reactive oxygen species and lactic acid (Nardi et al., 2005).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Elayaraja et al., 2014.

claim: Lactobacilli produce metabolites that are antibacterial in nature such as reactive oxygen species and lactic acid.
source: Lactobacilli produce antimicrobial peptides such as bacteriocins (Elayaraja et al., 2014) and metabolites that are antibacterial in nature such as reactive oxygen species and lactic acid (Nardi et al., 2005).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Nardi et al., 2005.

claim: Lactic acid was shown to inhibit growth of E. coli, S. enterica Typhimurium serovar, and L. monocytogenes.
source: Lactic acid was shown to inhibit growth of various bacterial pathogens; E. coli, S. enterica Typhimurium serovar, L. monocytogenes (De Keersmaecker et al., 2006; Wang et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to De Keersmaecker et al., 2006 and Wang et al., 2015.

claim: Lactic acid can penetrate cytoplasmic membranes in its non-dissociated form, which results in lowered cytoplasmic pH and disruption of the proton gradient across the cytoplasmic membrane.
source: This action is assigned to two mechanisms: (1) its capacity to penetrate cytoplasmic membranes in its non-dissociated form, which results in lowered cytoplasmic pH and disruption of the proton gradient across the cytoplasmic membrane (Alakomi et al., 2000); 2) its capacity to permeabilize the cytoplasmic membrane, which was proposed to increase in turn the sensitivity of lactic acid exposed bacteria (mainly gram-negative) to other antimicrobial compounds (Alakomi et al., 2000).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Alakomi et al., 2000.

claim: Lactic acid can permeabilize the cytoplasmic membrane, which was proposed to increase the sensitivity of lactic acid exposed bacteria to other antimicrobial compounds.
source: This action is assigned to two mechanisms: (1) its capacity to penetrate cytoplasmic membranes in its non-dissociated form, which results in lowered cytoplasmic pH and disruption of the proton gradient across the cytoplasmic membrane (Alakomi et al., 2000); 2) its capacity to permeabilize the cytoplasmic membrane, which was proposed to increase in turn the sensitivity of lactic acid exposed bacteria (mainly gram-negative) to other antimicrobial compounds (Alakomi et al., 2000).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Alakomi et al., 2000.

claim: Published reports indicate a broad antibacterial activity of L. murinus.
source: Published reports indicate a broad antibacterial activity of L. murinus (Bilkova et al., 2011; Perelmuter et al., 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Bilkova et al., 2011 and Perelmuter et al., 2008.

claim: The antimicrobial effect of L. murinus on S. aureus growth depends on low pH.
source: The antimicrobial effect of L. murinus on S. aureus growth depends on low pH as well (Bilkova et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Bilkova et al., 2011.

claim: S. pneumoniae colonization might require yet unknown anatomical conditions induced by commensal lung microbiota.
source: An explanation to this dilemma could be that S. pneumoniae colonization requires yet unknown anatomical conditions induced by commensal lung microbiota.
evidence: This is a speculation to explain the unexpected resistance of germ-free mice.

claim: One of the most prevalent KEGG pathways retrieved from the human tissue microbiome was carbohydrate metabolism.
source: One of the most prevalent KEGG pathways retrieved from the human tissue microbiome was carbohydrate metabolism (Yu et al., 2016), which includes the pathway involved in lactic acid generation.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Yu et al., 2016.

claim: Lactic acid levels in lungs are elevated under chronic inflammatory conditions as found in IPF patients.
source: Under chronic inflammatory conditions as found in IPF patients, lactic acid levels in lungs are elevated albeit the source of this lactate could not be determined (Kottmann et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Kottmann et al., 2012.

claim: In cystic fibrosis patients, neutrophils were identified as a source for lactic acid in sputum.
source: In cystic fibrosis patients, neutrophils were identified as a source for lactic acid in sputum (Bensel et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Bensel et al., 2011.

claim: L. murinus is not immunogenic when administered orally in mice.
source: In contrast to other Lactobacillus species (Ding et al., 2017) L. murinus is not immunogenic when administered orally in mice (Östberg et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Östberg et al., 2018.

claim: Lung tissue-associated microbiota of mice differ substantially from BALF microbiota, in containing large proportions of L. murinus.
source: Lung tissue-associated microbiota of mice differ substantially from BALF microbiota, in containing large proportions of L. murinus.
evidence: This is a conclusion stated in the Conclusions section based on the study's findings.

claim: Under dysbiotic conditions, intranasal instillation of L. murinus decreases the burden of S. pneumoniae colonization.
source: Under dysbiotic conditions, intranasal instillation of L. murinus decreases the burden of S. pneumoniae colonization.
evidence: This is a conclusion stated in the Conclusions section based on the study's findings.

claim: Probiotic treatment of bacterial lung infection might offer therapeutic alternatives in light of the ongoing antibiotic resistance crisis.
source: In light of the ongoing antibiotic resistance crisis, probiotic treatment of bacterial lung infection might offer therapeutic alternatives.
evidence: This is a speculation about potential clinical applications based on the study's findings.
